concepts.label: Work Done by a Constant Force
concepts.cardText: To lift a 5 kg bag of wheat slowly to a height of 1 m you must apply an upward force equal to mg, and the bag is displaced in the direction of the force; in everyday language you did some work. Lifting 3 bags, or applying a force 3 times larger over the same distance, does 3 times the work, and lifting a bag to 3 times the height with the same force also does 3 times the work. So the work done by a constant force is defined as the force applied multiplied by the displacement in the direction of the force, W = F x s. It is important to specify the force doing the work and the object on which the work is done. The SI unit of work is the joule (J): 1 joule of work is done when a constant force of 1 newton displaces an object by 1 metre in the direction of the force. On a force-displacement graph the work done equals the area under the graph, and this holds even when the force is not constant.

concepts.label: When Is the Work Done Zero?
concepts.cardText: No work is done on an object if the force acting on it is zero. The work done is also zero if there is no displacement of the object, regardless of the force applied; if you push a rigid wall there is no displacement in the wall and you have done no work on it. This may seem odd because you feel tired, but to apply a force the muscles in your body repeatedly expand and contract and use up the internal energy of your body, so in a scientific sense you have not done any work on the object. If a force acts in a direction perpendicular to the displacement, the work done by that force is zero because there is no displacement in the direction of the force; a girl carrying a box horizontally applies an upward force to balance its weight, so this force does no work on the box.

concepts.label: Positive and Negative Work
concepts.cardText: The work done by a force on an object can be positive or negative, depending on the relative directions of the force and the displacement. When the displacement is in the same direction as the applied force the work done is positive, as when you push a wheelchair. When the displacement is in the direction opposite to that of the force the work done is negative, as when a goalkeeper stops a ball by applying a force opposite to the motion of the football. Force and displacement have both magnitude and direction, but work does not have a direction; it can be described by a number with a positive or negative sign. When a girl lifts a dumbbell up the force is in the direction of displacement, so she does positive work, and when she lowers it the force she applies is opposite to the displacement, so she does negative work. In Example 7.2 the goalkeeper's hand moves back 15 cm as she applies 200 N, so the work done on the ball is 200 N times minus 0.15 m, which is minus 30 J. The ball and the goalkeeper apply equal and opposite forces on each other: the ball does positive work on the goalkeeper while she does negative work on the ball.

concepts.label: The Work-Energy Theorem
concepts.cardText: A cricket ball thrown towards the wicket can make the wicket fall, and a flowerpot raised to a height can damage an object below it when it falls; in each case the object has acquired a capacity to do work. An object having the capacity to do work is said to possess energy. The ball gained its energy from the work done by the fielder in throwing it, and the pot from the work done in raising it. When positive work is done on an object it gains energy, which it can transfer by applying a force on another object. Work done on an object appears as a change in its energy; this relation is called the work-energy theorem: work done on an object equals the change in its energy. The theorem also holds for a system of objects or when the forces are not constant. The SI unit of energy is the joule, the same as work. Mechanical work is one way of transferring energy, but energy can also be transferred as heat from a hotter to a colder object, through radiation like the Sun's energy, in electric circuits, by sound waves and in nuclear reactions.

concepts.label: Forms of Energy
concepts.cardText: Energy is the capacity to do work. The examples so far correspond to mechanical energy, but energy can exist in many other forms: thermal, light, sound, electrical, chemical and nuclear energy. It is possible to change energy from one form to another. Electrical energy is converted into light energy in a bulb and into thermal energy of the water in an electric water heater. The chemical energy in the food we eat powers our muscles and gets converted into mechanical energy, and a ringing bell converts mechanical energy into sound energy. Mechanical energy is the energy that an object possesses due to its motion or position.

concepts.label: Kinetic Energy
concepts.cardText: The energy possessed by an object due to its motion is called kinetic energy. All moving objects possess kinetic energy, such as a moving bicycle or a rolling ball, and an object that does not move is defined to have zero kinetic energy. For an object starting from rest and acquiring a velocity under a force, the work done by the force equals the energy gained, which is its kinetic energy. For an object of mass m moving with velocity v the kinetic energy is half m v squared, in joules. Kinetic energy has no direction. When positive work is done on an object and its velocity increases, its kinetic energy increases; if negative work is done and its velocity decreases, its kinetic energy decreases; and if no work is done and the velocity does not change, the kinetic energy remains constant. If the velocity of a vehicle doubles in magnitude, its kinetic energy becomes 4 times the original value. In Example 7.6 the wire of an aircraft carrier exerts a backward force on a landing jet, doing negative work that reduces its kinetic energy to zero.

concepts.label: Potential Energy
concepts.cardText: When a stretched band or a bent bow is released it applies a force on the object in contact with it and sets it in motion. The stack of coins, the ball or the arrow gain kinetic energy they did not originally possess, and this must have come from the stretched band or bent bow, which have the capacity to do work due to their shape; the work done in deforming them was stored. A stretched or compressed spring likewise stores energy while it is in a deformed state, and when released transfers it to the kinetic energy of the object in contact. Internal forces allow energy to be stored in a deformed object. Energy can also be stored by changing the arrangement of objects in a system: separated unlike magnets, or separated electric charges, store energy due to their relative positions, and so does a ball lifted away from the Earth. Whenever a system of objects interacts through forces, such as gravitational, electric or magnetic forces, it can store energy due to the relative positions of the objects. The energy stored by an object as a result of its deformation or in a system of objects due to their relative positions is called potential energy.

concepts.label: Gravitational Potential Energy
concepts.cardText: The stored energy of the Earth-ball system is often simply called the gravitational potential energy of the ball, and in this chapter potential energy usually means gravitational potential energy. In Activity 7.1 a heavy ball dropped on sand from a greater height makes a deeper depression, because raising a ball to a greater height requires more work and so the ball possesses more energy at a greater height: the greater the height of the ball above the Earth's surface, the greater is its potential energy. To raise an object of mass m gradually to a height h we apply a force equal to mg, so the work done is mgh, and by the work-energy theorem this appears as a change in potential energy, giving U = mgh. The unit of potential energy is the joule, the same as work or kinetic energy. Work done against gravitational, electric or magnetic forces can be stored as potential energy, but work done against friction does not lead to a storage of energy. The expression mgh is valid only near the Earth's surface.

concepts.label: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
concepts.cardText: The sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy of an object is called its mechanical energy. For an object dropped from height h, at the top the potential energy is mgh and the kinetic energy is zero, so the mechanical energy is mgh. As it falls, its potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases; the increase in kinetic energy equals the decrease in potential energy, so the lost potential energy is converted into kinetic energy while the mechanical energy remains constant. As an object moves due to the gravitational force, its mechanical energy remains the same if no other external forces act on it; this is called the conservation of mechanical energy. A pendulum bob reaches almost the same height it started with, which shows its mechanical energy is conserved, but in real life it slows down and stops because of energy lost to friction at the support and air resistance. Using conservation of mechanical energy, the child at the bottom of a slide of height h has a velocity that depends only on the height, so the shape of the slide or the mass of the child should not matter, neglecting friction. Conservation of mechanical energy may offer a simpler route than Newton's laws, and the total energy of a system not acted upon by external forces stays constant.

concepts.label: Power
concepts.cardText: Running up the stairs in one minute feels very different from walking up slowly in five minutes, even though the same work is done in both cases; this difference is described by power. Power is defined as the rate at which work is done: the average power is the work done divided by the time taken. To do more work in the same time interval requires more power, and to do the same work in a shorter time also requires more power. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 watt is 1 joule of work done per second, named after James Watt, who invented an efficient steam engine. Another unit, the horsepower, equals 746 W and was used because early engines were compared with the power of horses.

concepts.label: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage
concepts.cardText: Although the total work required for a task cannot be reduced, it can be made easier by changing the magnitude or direction of the force that needs to be applied. The devices that help us do this are called simple machines; the chapter studies the pulley, the inclined plane and the lever. The force we apply to a machine is called the effort, and the force that needs to be overcome is called the load. To describe how a machine changes the magnitude of the applied force, mechanical advantage is defined as the ratio of the load to the effort. Simple machines make work easier by changing the magnitude or direction of the force, though they do not reduce total work. Machines do not create energy; they only help us use it more effectively, and the work we put in equals the useful work done on the load, ignoring friction. Many machines in daily life are made up of two or more simple machines.

concepts.label: The Pulley
concepts.cardText: A pulley is a wheel with a groove that guides a rope. A fixed pulley, as used to raise a flag, does not reduce the magnitude of the force required; it only changes its direction. It is easier for us to pull downward than to lift a load by applying an upward force directly, so the pulley provides convenience by changing the direction of the effort. Since the effort and the load are equal in magnitude, the mechanical advantage of a fixed pulley is 1. Movable pulleys, or a system of pulleys, can have a mechanical advantage greater than 1 and can lift much heavier objects with much smaller effort; in a movable pulley system the load is attached to the movable pulley and one end of the rope is fixed. Pulleys are widely used in elevators and cranes.

concepts.label: The Inclined Plane
concepts.cardText: An inclined plane is a simple machine that helps move a heavy load to a higher (or lower) level. In Activity 7.3 the force needed to pull a cart up to the height of a pile of books decreases as the plank becomes less steep, but the force must be applied over a larger distance to reach the same height. If an object is moved at constant speed up an inclined plane of length L to a height h, the work done is the effort times L and the potential energy gained is mgh; by the work-energy theorem, ignoring friction, effort times L equals mgh. Since L is larger than h, the effort is less than the load mg and the mechanical advantage of the inclined plane is greater than 1, and a longer, shallower plane reduces the effort further. The work done, the product of force and displacement, is the same in all cases: if the force decreases the displacement increases, so the work stays constant.

concepts.label: The Lever
concepts.cardText: A lever is a rigid bar that can rotate about a fixed point. It has three main parts: the fulcrum, a fixed point about which the lever rotates; the load, the force to be overcome; and the effort, the force applied. The distance of the load from the fulcrum is the load arm and the distance of the effort from the fulcrum is the effort arm. The end of the lever on which the smaller force is applied moves a larger distance, while the other end, which applies a larger force to lift a heavier object, moves a smaller distance; the work done on one end is transferred to the other, so F1 x d1 = F2 x d2. A beam balance is a lever, and it balances when effort x effort arm = load x load arm. If the effort arm is increased, the effort required to move the same load is reduced, and the mechanical advantage of a lever is the ratio of the effort arm to the load arm. The effort required is generally smaller but has to move a larger distance, so a lever reduces the force required but not the total work done. Levers are of three classes depending on the relative positions of the effort, fulcrum and load.
